title: Learning with a teacher
hook: the student reads the line perfectly, and the teacher says: again
tomorrow: can an English translation hand you the Guru's words?

segments.voice: Last week, the page itself: signs, dots, spaces, headings, the center, the numbers, and yesterday, many forms. A lot for one reader to catch alone. So who catches the sounds you get wrong?

Voice-to-text hears you say one thing and types another, and it never knows. Saturday morning, a side room at a gurdwara. A teacher and a student sit knee to knee over one gutka. The teacher reads a line of the Japji. The student reads it back. The teacher's hand lifts: that sound, again. The student fixes it and reads the line through, clean, every sign in place. The student waits to move on. And the teacher says, gently: again.
screen: `VOICE-TO-TEXT NEVER KNOWS.` → `KNEE TO KNEE OVER ONE GUTKA.` → `CLEAN. AND THE TEACHER SAYS: AGAIN.`

segments.voice: This is santhiaa: learning to read the Guru's words aloud with a teacher who hears each sound. Everything from last week lives here. Where a larivaar line breaks into words. Which small sign is said, and which is barely breathed. And something the page can't show at all: vishraam, the places to pause inside a line, so the meaning lands the right way. Those are learned by ear, from someone who learned them by ear. So why again, after a clean reading? Because santhiaa isn't only catching mistakes. A line read right once is borrowed. Read right many times, it settles, and the sound becomes yours to carry. Guru Nanak says it in the Japji, in paraphrase: within the mind are gems and jewels and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. Listening comes first. The student's ear is learning from the teacher's ear. Here's the thing to tell a friend: some of the most careful reading of the Granth isn't done by eyes alone. It's done by two people sitting close, one reading, one listening, repeating a line until the sound is settled in both of them.
screen: `SANTHIAA: A TEACHER WHO HEARS.` · `VISHRAAM: WHERE TO PAUSE.` · `AGAIN, UNTIL IT SETTLES.` · `LISTENING COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `A TEACHER'S EAR.`

segments.voice: Read one short line aloud, the Japji's opening or any line you've been learning, and record it on your phone if you can. Play it back once and listen like a teacher: a sound that slipped, a pause in the wrong place. Then read it again, slower, and let that second reading be the one you keep.
Santhiaa: learning to read the Guru Granth Sahib aloud correctly, sound by sound and pause by pause, with a teacher listening. The tenth word of the year.
Your line: a teacher's ear. It catches what your own ear can't. Ten of twenty, and a new week.

screen: `DAY 1436 COUNTS.` → `READING THE GRANTH · 10 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: CAN AN ENGLISH TRANSLATION HAND YOU THE GURU'S WORDS?`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs learn to read Gurbani through santhiaa: a teacher, at a gurdwara or at home, reads each line and the student repeats it until the pronunciation and the pauses are correct.

santhiaa.meaning: learning to read Gurbani aloud correctly with a teacher

vishraam.meaning: a pause inside a line of Gurbani, placed for meaning

gutka.meaning: a small book of the daily prayers

larivaar.meaning: the Granth's words written joined, with no spaces

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's hymn at the opening of the Granth
